A few votes of that kind might be recorded and counted promiscuously throughout the whole electoral district, and would not be of much consequence, but the colonization of them in some particular 'locality might have the effect of turning the scale. We should have some provision with reference to minors. A young man who enlists for overseas is supposed to be 18. Why go under that age? Some are under 18. Under this Bill, you may have a minor ten years old, or five years old or an infant in arms. Of course, they would not vote, but you are leaving the door open to an opportunity for wrong-doing, and that opportunity should not be given in a measure such as this providing for the peace, order and good government of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I quite agree with the hon. gentleman, at all events, in one respect, that is, that there are two distinct questions involved here: First, should we give the vote to the soldier who had not been a resident of Canada? Second, if we do give him a vote, then where are we going to allot his vote? The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) warned me as to what I would have to consent to being suspected of if I adhered to this proposal, and he expressed a great deal of scandalized horror that the proposal should have been made. As regards giving the vote to the soldier, even although he had not resided in Canada, I gave, before the committee rose at six o'clock, some reasons which, in my judgment, seemed to quite justify that action on our part. A great deal is made of this question of non-residence in Canada. My hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) has demonstrated that there are to-day in some parts of this country, and there certainly have been in the past-and not a very remote past-in other parts of this country, a perfect recognition of the right of the British subject, non-resident in Canada, when he has certain other qualifications, to vote. In Quebec, until 1912, when

we had the introduction of the "one man, one vote," and when in consequence there were certain modifications made, including,
I believe, the requirement of residence for the exercise of the franchise I am not saying that positively, because I have not had occasion to look very carefully into the statute-the British subject, who owned real property in that province, was an elector in that province and, being such, was an elector in this Dominion, Not only does that result from the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act from which the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) read, making the lists provided by the provinces valid lists, but we have a special section of the Dominion Elections Act still in force recognizing the right of non-residents to vote! and it is headed "Non-resident electors," and provides that:
The provisions of the law of the province as to the places where non-resident electors shall vote shall apply mutatis mutandis to any Dominion election, and the returning officer at such election shall have the powers and he charged with the duties of the sheriff or returning officer under such provisions; but nothing herein shall enable any person to vote by schedule or otherwise than by appearing personally.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Is that vote counted
except on a recount?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
That vote is counted.
That man presents himself at the poll and registers his vote. What is guarded against is anybody voting otherwise than by presenting himself personally at the poll. But the fact that, as I understand it, still in Nova Scotia and certainly prior to the time to which I referred in Quebec, a person, being a British subject and a property holder in a constituency in one of those provinces, had never resided in the Dominion would not prevent him, if he came over and presented himself at the poll, 'from registering his vote. I mention this only to point out that this is not the astounding innovation that is suggested.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It is a mistake to say
that a non-resident in Quebec who is a property holder has a right to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I am not stating that
that is so at the present time.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: He must be a resident.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will follow me-I have under my hand the Quebec statute of 1912 which modified the law in that regard, but the law, as it stood before 1912, not only recognized the possibility but expressly declared that people who
had not been resident for a year past in the province, with the exception of proprietors of real estate, should not be entitled to vote. The statute of 1912, by which the "one man, one vote" system was introduced, amended that law by striking out the exception, so that I am not contending that to-day it is so. I am pointing this out only to show that this is not the extraordinary innovation that is suggested. It follows that residence has not been a universal provision; at all events, it has not been looked upon in the past in this country and to a certain extent at present it is not looked upon in this country as an essential qualification for voting. There is room for difference of opinion, but I am not going to be led into discussions about motives. If it does anybody's heart good to suspect ,me of evil motives in this regard, then I hope his heart may rejoice to its full extent.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
We shall say that the
minister is absolutely innocent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I hope the hon. gentleman on the other side who smiles at that assurance will derive all imaginable happiness from the confidence and the conviction that my motives are of the very worst. That will not alter what is right or wrong about this question. The question as to giving the right to vote after all comes back to this: Does a man, by constituting himself a member of the Canadian Forces and risking his life for the defence of Canada, giving to Canada the credit and the glory of whatever he may achieve, link himself sufficiently with Canada to entitle him to be put upon a footing with any British subject who may steal into this country looking to make some money and settle down in some place for five or six months with a view to earning what he can earn there, and who may go away the next day. I am not saying that the argument is all on one side, but it seems to me that the soldier, under those circumstances, has as intimately connected himself with Canada and has, in addition, demonstrated that his desire is that the connection on his part should be one of service and of sacrifice as has the gentleman, who has come in here merely for his own pleasure or his own profit, and certainly demonstrated that his desire for connection with Canada has not as its basis any desire to be of service to Canada. That it is a proper thing to give the vote to the soldier-I still cannot get away from the conviction, even at the risk of having imputed to me the motives that are suggested, that it is the proper thing to give

him the vote, both because he deserves it and because it is good policy on Canada's part to try to bind to herself the manwhohas given such evidence of desiring to be a serving citizen of Canada-that is one question.
The other question is, if we are right in giving them the vote, how are we going to deal with the allocation of the votes? In giving the vote, I would point out that we are not in reality making a substantial departure from the provision of the Act as it stands, because, although that provision requires thirty days residence in Canada before enlistment, all the objections that are made to giving a vote to a man who never resided in Canada surely apply with equal force' to the man who has been but thirty days in Canada before enlisting. Is there any remarkable difference, as to then-knowledge of political questions and the candidates and the constituencies, between the man who came into Canada the day before he enlisted, and the man who came in thirty days before he enlisted? The provision of the present Act has been spoken of as being eminently fair, and was agreed to by this House when the Act Was passed.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The man who had resided in Canada thirty days before enlisting would know w'hat section of the country he was in.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: He might have that knowledge without having knowledge of the name of the constituency. But I understood the objection of my hon. friend .to rest mainly on the question of allowing him to select his own constituency. I understood that also to be the main objection of my hon. friend from Welland, and I was endeavouring to point out that these were two perfectly distinct questions. I am quite prepared to admit that there is possibility of abuse under the system that allows a man to indicate the place where he may vote, but there is possibility of abuse, I think, under any system which lye adopt with regard to that man; and if you adopt the system-and we 'have thought of many different systems-of saying that he shall vote in the constituency in which he enlisted, you have not only the possibility, but the certainty, of hiving, because it happens that in certain constituencies of this country there were very large enlistments of people who came from different places.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Since the Soldiers' Voting Bill was passed we have had a Redistribution Bill, and a certain portion of [ Mr. Doherty. ]
the county of Laval has been divided into four pa,rts, one part forming the new division of St. Denis, and the other three parts being annexed respectively to Two Mountains, Jacques Cartier >and Maisonneuve. I feel satisfied that some of my constituents who are at the front would not know what constituency they were in. It seems to me that instead of the soldier being allowed to make his choice, his vote should be cast in the parish from which he enlisted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will allow me to dispose of one question at a time, I will conclude what I was endeavouring to say, and then be very glad to deal with his question. We did consider different systems, notwithstanding that we were intent, according to the hon. member for St. John, upon finding a method whereby fraud could be committed. We looked at the different systems with a view to finding a practical way out, and we have not closed any door yet. The hon. member for St. John may be as offensive as he knows how -and that is saying a good deal-but he will not succeed in inducing me to close a door to anything that will insure a fairer application of this law in my judgment than the present draft does. I give him carte blanche, let his language be as strong as he likes. I am here to get through the House a .measure which, as I lay it before hon. gentlemen, I do not believe to be perfect, but which was intended to produce the result I announced at the outset, of securing the vote for as many of our soldiers as possible, surrounding it with all possible safeguards, but not so as to make it practically impossible for anything like a full vote to be taken.
Let us suppose for ia moment that, with the exception of myself, everybody is trying to find a fair way of doing this thing. I am the man that was found out by the hon. member for St. John-

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The man whose Bill was found out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Let us put it that way; the hon. gentleman is beginning to moderate. What are you going to do with that eoldier vote? Are you going to hive all the votes in the places where the soldiers happen to have enlisted? Is that fair to the constituencies where the largest enrollment took place? Is it fair that because they attracted soldiers, and got a large number of enlistments, that all these men should be forcibly put upon them? I understand that many of these men would be in the

position pointed out toy the hon. member for Laval, and would have difficulty of their own knowledge in defining the limits of particular constituencies in Canada, but I hardly think that they would have passed the period of training, which in many cases extends over a period of six months, without finding out something, if not about the electoral divisions/, at least about the village or town or city in which they enlisted; and if they found that out, they would at least know something of that constituency. I do not think it unreasonable to suppose that they would hit upon the particular constituency in which they enlisted. But that is one thing, and it is another thing to impose them absolutely on that constituency.
One suggestion was, that we allocate the votes to the places where the soldiers enlisted. If we did that, we /should have an undue proportion of these men landed into constituencies which happened to be good enlisting centres. The suggestion was also made that these soldiers should be made to vote at the address that they gave in their attestation papers, and I may say that that was a method that suggested itself as having much to commend it, and I believe it was the method that was adopted in Australia, but we did not get very far with that before it was pointed out that with that too, you would get an undue proportion- a large number of drifting people, so to speak-who would give their address as being in the place where they attested.
For instance, with regard to the first contingent that system would probably have captured for somebody the county of Quebec, because in and around Valcartier there would have been a large number of people who never had any connection with that county at all, but who had named as their addresses certain places in that neighbourhood. So that there, instead of creating the possibility of hiving people, you were getting a certainty of hiving people. It is possible that some people may endeavour to use influence to induce these men who are given the opportunity of indicating their place of voting to vote in one place rather than in another. But before we get through with this Bill we will see that there is the same opportunity for exercising that influence on the part of one party as there is on the part of another. It is true that the presiding officers are, as in this country the returning officers are, to be named by the Government, and that the presiding officers are to name the deputy presiding officers, just as in this country the returning officer names the deputy
returning officer. But provisions are made to secure representation for the different parties interested. All these presiding and deputy presiding officers are to be taken in the military forces; all this is to be done within what might be called the military home. Why is it presumed that there will be greater power on the part of one party than on the part of another to indicate places which they would desire these men to select as their places of voting? The field is open, I have no doubt that there may be requests, solicitations or suggestions that the men vote in one place rather than in another. But why we should have reason to anticipate that, from one side more than from the other, there should be an endeavour to concentrate these people on any particular constituencies, I am quite at a loss to see. When we cannot find any method of defining where these people are voting, without actually by the law itself making them swamp some particular constituencies, why should we think that it would be a greater evil that that might possibly happen under this system than that it would certainly happen under the other? I do not want to close the door upon any suggestion that will meet the real difficulty that presents itself. For my part, I think that these men ought to be given the vote. As has been pointed out, this legislation is only for an election that may be held during the present war. We are not going to make these men voters forever; we are going to recognize them as voters so long as they are soldiers.
Mr. GERMAN; But their votes will have an'effect long after this war is finished.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: So long as there is a general election during the war, not a byelection?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Not a by-election, no. But to answer the question of the member for Laval: I quite believe that a large number of soldiers who have actually been resident in Canada will not be able to give the name of their electoral division. I could pick out numbers of people in the city of Montreal who, I am quite satisfied, if somebody did not explain to them once in a while when an election is coming on where the boundary line runs between St. Anne and St. Antoine, would not be quite sure whether they were voters in the one district or in the other. And there will be soldiers on the other side who will not be able to give that information. But we have not left the matter in the position in which the hon. member for Laval supposes it to

be. Subsection 2 of section 3 reads as follows:
If he can state the electoral district wherein he last continuously resided during at least
	 months of the year immediately
preceding his appointment, enlistment, enrolment or calling out on active service, or so particularly specify a place or places within an electoral district whereat during such period of time he so resided that such electoral district can therefrom he ascertained, he shall be deemed an elector of the electoral district so stated or to be ascertained, and his vote shall be applied thereto.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is what I object to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman object that the man will not be able to indicate his electoral district?

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: What I object to is that a man who was resident in the county of Laval as it stood before redistribution should choose as his place of voting any part of that county that now belongs to another constituency. I wish his name to remain on the lists of the electoral district in which he lived; then he will be bound to vote in that electoral district. I want him to have the privilege of voting, but under this measure the cavil or military authorities can say whiat part of the county that man comes from, and he will have to vote there, notwithstanding that it may now be in another electoral division.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Suppose a gentleman
resided in the village of Ste. Rose, which is in the county of Laval. There has been a redistribution. That gentleman now knows that he lived in the village of Ste. Rose, but he does not know in what electoral district that is. In that case, he will say: I resided in the village of Ste. Rose for such a period of time. From that statement that he resided in the village of Ste. Rose, the electoral county to which he belongs can be ascertained. The fact that he stated that he resided in the village of Ste. Rose will be on the back of the envelope in which his ballot is contained. The first operation of the returning officer to whom that-goes is to assort the ballots, and he will see on the back of that ballot that this man resided in the village of Ste. Rose. He will be provided by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery with the necessary charts and documents showing the limitations of the constituency. He will turn to those and see that the village of Ste. Rose is in the present constituency of-whatever it may be. That envelope, unopened, will be assorted with the votes for the county in which the village of Ste. Rose is situated and the

man's ballot will be counted in that very county in which he as a resident of Ste. Rose belongs. The only man who is to have a chance to indicate where he desires to vote is the man who neither knows the name of his electoral constituency or is in a position to name a place or places in which he resided or from the naming of which the constituency can be ascertained. In the case suggested the man was in a position to tell where he resided. He will be asked where he resided, not merely in what electoral district he resided.
If he says, "I resided in such a county," we know as far as he can tell us. If he says, "I cannot tell the county," he will be asked, "What place did you reside in?" In the instance mentioned, he will give Ste. Rose and Ste. Rose will give the constituency. You may have to get more particulars when you get into city constituencies, such as streets and numbers. From streets and numbers you will ascertain by reference to charts, which have been prepared showing the limits as fixed by the Redistribution Act, in what constituency the man is. There is no ground to apprehend difficulty in so far as regards a man who knows where he lives, whether he knows the name of the constituency or not; that man will vote in the constituency in which he lives.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Except that he is required to select the district.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If my hon. friend expects to find in this section all the provisions of the law I am afraid he will not find them because this does not say so.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If the minister will kindly look at form B, page 16, he will find the following:
6.	Specify the names of the place or places in Canada (giving streets and numbers when possible) whereat you last continuously resided during at least.... months of the year immediately preceding your appointment, enlistment, enrolment or calling out on active service.
7.	State if you can the electoral district wherein such place or places in which you so resided are situate.
Electoral district	
Province	
8.	If because of non-residence or otherwise you cannot specify or state as required by Questions No. 6 and No. 7, to what electoral district do you desire your vote to be applied?
Unless he can answer both 6 and 7 then he selects his own district.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If he cannot answer 6 and 7 he shall elect; that is if he can answer neither one nor the other.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If he can answer either one then he is not in a position where he cannot answer one or the other.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Unless he answers both he selects his own district.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: This is brought to my attention in the middle of the discussion of another section. It is possible that the word "and" should be "or" and perhaps we will have to make it "or" when we get to it. But if we could keep to the section we are dealing with, possibly we could get at a practical result. I am anxious to receive criticisms and suggestions in a good spirit and try to meet them. I would remind hon. gentlemen that it is the section that makes the law, the form should comply with the section and if it does not, we will have to correct it.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If the language of the law was as plain as tUe language of the minister, I would not complain. But what is reported in Hansard is not the law. What will be brought before the courts and before the electors will be this Bill after it is passed. I cannot read subsection 3 in any other way than as it is set down here.
If he cannot, because of non-residence or otherwise-
Or otherwise.
-so state or specify, he shall be deemed an ^lector of, and his vote shall be applied to, such electoral district as he may indicate.
Supposing he says "I am a resident of Ste. Rose; I do not know in what county it is now, and I do not care"-what county do you choose? If a man so state or specify his vote shall be applied by somebody, not himself, to such electoral district as he may indicate. ,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman wall read what the voter has to state or specify, he will see that it is one or other of two things. In subsection 2 we have no trouble about our conjunction:
2. If he can state the electoral district wherein he last continuously resided during at least	months of the year immediately preceding his appointment, enlistment, enrolment or calling out on active service, or so particularly specify a place or places within an electoral district whereat during such period of time he so resided that such electoral district can therefrom be ascertained, he shall be deemed an elector of the electoral district so stated or to be ascertained, and his vote shall be applied thereto.
Subsection 3 is for the man who cannot state his electoral district and who cannot specify the name or place where he resided so that from the name or place it will be
possible for the electoral district :to be ascertained. If he can do either one or other of these two things the subsection does not apply to him. It iis only if he can do neither of these two things that subsection 3 applies.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The minister ignores the form altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The form is not in the present section and we are dealing with the section. If the form has not been printed to conform to the section, we will amend the form when we reach it.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: What would the minister suggest will be the procedure with regard to the man who says: "I am from the United States; I do not know anything about the electoral districts of Canada; I want to vote and I want to vote for the Government," let us say. "I do not care where I vote." How will you apply that vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If he cannot give information under section 2 which will indicate where he would like to vote, I am afraid he will have to do without voting. This is a Bill to afford an opportunity of voting; but it is not a Bill to compel people to vote. We are providing not to take the horse to the water but to take the water to the horse, and when we have got it there we cannot make the horse drink. If a man will not indicate any constituency you cannot make him vote.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: He does not know any.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I should think that a man who desired to vote and who had the right to select a constituency would ascertain from his comrades.
I should think that, if he cared to vote, he would ascertain the name of some constituency from the other soldiers or from the representatives of the two parties who would be present. His one desire would be to register a Canadian vote, and he would have no trouble in ascertaining the name of a constituency.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is the difficulty; he will have no trouble, but he will be influenced entirely by the officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
As things are in our elections at home people are apt to be influenced by men all around them. Is it a serious objection that a man should be asked to vote in a certain constituency? Perhaps I would say to him: I would be glad to have you vote in Ste. Anne, and



the hon. member for North Oxford might say that he would be glad to have him vote elsewhere.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Or out in the Yukon; some place where there is a very narrow vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If it is right to give him the privilege of voting, are we to refuse to him that right because he may be influenced in its exercise? At that rate we would have to refuse the ballot to every voter in this country.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Supposing it was suggested that every Canadian soldier, although he has a residence in Canada, should be permitted to select his constituency anywhere in Canada. Why not give him the same privilege that you give to the American, the non-resident?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Because it is possible to attach the man who has resided in Canada to a constituency.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: But why treat him worse than you treat the non-resident?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Because if we could
pick out a constituency for the other voter we would do so.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The minister must think it an evil to allow a man to pick out any one of the 230 constituencies in Canada and to allocate his vote to it, and yet he proposes to give to the non-resident that right, although he may have no interest in the future of Canada.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that a man, even although not a native-born Canadian, who has'come to this country and enlisted and gone overseas, might have no interest in the future of Canada? That was the hon. gentleman's statement.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I have not said that.
The Bill does not limit it to the case of a non-resident who has come to Canada to enlist, but extends the right to a man who may have enlisted in England. He may never have set foot in Canada. He may have enlisted in the Bermudas, and yet, because he attaches himself to the Canadian Expeditionary Force, he is permitted by this Bill to vote and to select his own constituency in any part of Canada.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Would my hon. friend not allow that man to vote?

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am opposed to giving the vote to any man who has not been a resident of Canada. Yes.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am veTy glad to have my hon. friend on record.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I have been on record
all afternoon.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN. The Bill defines military voters to include all members of the military forces mentioned here, or anyone who has been honourably discharged therefrom. Some 65,900 men were discharged from the Canadian forces up to the 14th of June who never proceeded overseas. I assume that they have obtained discharges, although I am not sure. Under this section they would be military electors in this country. Supposing 20 peT cent of them were under age, that is under twenty-one . yeaTS of age, that would mean that 13.000 or 14,000 of these people in Canada would have votes.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
As a matter of fact,
how many are there?

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I do not know,
but I assume 20 per cent. Many of these would be in the force from a few days to six months, and the -question arises in my mind whether it is necessary or proper that they should be made, by statute, military electors in Canada. Many of them never intended to proceed overseas. I think the provision should be modified in some way. Then there were discharged in England, up to June 30, some 4,380 men. I assume that these were British-born who 'enlisted in Canada and proceeded overseas with various regiments, men who were entitled to toe discharged in Canada but preferred taking their discharge in England 'because they intended again taking up residence there. It is worth the minister's while considering whether these should be qualified as electors in Canada under this section.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: A number of those men were probably discharged in England for the purpose of taking out commissions in either the Canadian or the Imperial army.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I should like the minister to keep these two points in mind. I wish he would explain what is covered by the auxiliary motor boat patrol service. Is that service organized, and, if so, where does it exist? Is it to proceed overseas?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It is overseas.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: In what position is the Canadian soldier, having enlisted here, but having gone overseas and been transferred from the Canadian force to a branch of the Imperial Army?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Under the section in the Bill as introduced, the vote would not be extended to Canadians who form part of the Imperial Force. As, I explained when the Bill was introduced, the reason we had not included Canadians in the Imperial service was that we 'had not been able to devise means whereby we would be able to take their votes. A suggestion was made when I introduced the Bill which led to further consideration being given, and we have reached a conclusion to amend this definition, so as to include men of Canadian citizenship serving in Imperial forces. We might not be able to find the men, and the presiding officer might not be in a position to obtain their vote. We shall amend the section to. meet that case.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The Bill says that every military elector shall be qualified and entitled to vote at a general election. That is quite clear, and then the Bill tells us what a military elector is. The section reads:	.
"Military elector" means and includes every person, male or female, who, being a British subject, whether or not ordinarily resident in ada., appointed, enlisted, enrolled or called out dian, has been, while within or without Canada, appointed, enlisted, enrolled or caVed out for active service as one of the Canadian Expeditionary Force.
My two points are on the words "minor" and on the words "called out". Under the ordinary law in our province an elector must be 21 years of age and a British subject
There are some other provisos.
10 p.m. but the age must be 21. I
desire to ask if this Bill is applicable to ithe conscription law, because, under section 2 of the Military Service Bill, the Government will take the right to call out classes of the ages 20 to 35. If the Government calls out classes 1 or 2, that will include everybody who will be conscripted, and it will also call out electors who would otherwise have been considered minors. Thousands of young men would be called out. I am not opposed to these young men having a vote, but it would make a big difference in the city of Montreal. It would be interesting to know that at any moment the Government could put in a constituency like mine thousands of ' young men, who, I thought would have no vote. I should like to know, if this measure is applicable to the conscription law, because I see in clause 2 of the Military Service Bill the words:
2. (1) Every male British subject who comes within one of the classes described in section three of this Act, shall be liable to be called out as hereinafter provided on active service in the Canadian Expeditionary Force for the defence of Canada.
These are exactly the same words as in the Bill before us. If this Bill is passed, thousands and thousands of young men in my hon. friend's district in Montreal could be called out and given a vote. I should like to know if that is going to be done. I might go a little further than my hon. friend from Welland who. speaks of three votes in each of 60 different polling subdivisions, which give ia total of 180 votes. We might have a good many more votes in each division in Montreal than my hon. friend from Welland suggests.
I was going to raise the point suggested by my hon. friend from Halifax, in regard to the discharged soldiers who are not 21 years of age. They have enrolled from the age of 18 up, and the Government could put a lot of voters in the different divisions of Montreal and in other places, because, in my opinion, at any time the Governor in Council by proclamation could call out on active service, as aforesaid, for the defence of Canada-exactly the same words as in the other Bill -thousands of young men would have a vote, three weeks before polling day. I desire an explanation on that point, because I want to know where I stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I might first deal with the question asked by the hon. gentleman from Halifax. I understand his first question to be whether it was intended that the honourably discharged soldier should have the vote as a military voter. I may say that was the intention, and I think that is the effect of the section. The intention was that the military vote should belong, not only to the soldier actually in the performance of his duty, but to the man vho has been a soldier. The principle object in view was to assure the vote to the returned soldier, but it operates, and it was intended to operate, so that the vote could be secured to the honourably discharged soldier. It is quite true that the provision may operate to give a vote to a certain number of soldiers whose service was, perhaps, of not very great value, but it will only be such soldiers as gave the service that they were .able to give, and ceased to be soldiers simply because they were honourably discharged from service. It is true they have not done anything in the way of actual service to be compared

to the men who have actually carried the work through and been to the front, but on the other hand, is it an undue consideration to give to the man who was willing to be a soldier, who, so far as it depended upon himself, did everything within his power, and was, at all events, sufficiently qualified that he succeeded in passing the first examination at the time of enrolment or enlistment? It may be and, I dare say, it is quite true that amongst those young men could be found some who did themselves know of or who suspected their disqualification and who did not anticipate going overseas, but if that were done under conditions in which one could be quite satisfied that in the particular case the individual had been guilty of conduct such as that, I doubt if he would be honourably discharged.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Why not remove the qualification so far as such a man is concerned? This Bill is not intended to cover the case of such men. They are under no disability. It is true they joined the service, but they were struck off the ' strength later on and they never went overseas. Why include them within the scope of this Bill? I suppose most of the men struck off the strength and over 21 wdll have votes in any case. After being struck off the strength, they will return to their own homes, so that all who will have the vote will be minors. It is rather objectionable to have minors vote in some electoral districts of Canada when other minors are not permitted to vote. Amongst that list you might find a small number of women who enlisted for hospital service overseas, but who were unable to proceed overseas for one cause or another. I do not think it is advisable to have them enrolled as electors in the forthcoming Election.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
There is a provision
later on under which men in that position in Canada, honourably discharged soldiers, are declared to be entitled to vote in the constituency in which they reside. They are entitled to have their ballots taken upon their affidavit and upon production of the certificates of their enrolment and their honourable discharge, so that no confusion is caused. Such a man will not be on the list.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: His name will not be on the list?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
No, but under the
statute he will be entitled to vote upon presenting himself, upon producing the evidence of his discharge and making affidavit as to his identity with the person mentioned in the documents. It will be the case of a man voting who is not upon the list. I do not see that there is any great anomaly in allowing this young man who is a minor, even although he be in Canada, to vote, while other minors in Canada are not voting. There is this substantial difference between the minor we are dealing with and the other minors in the constituency, that this particular minor has, at all events so far as within him lay, been a Canadian soldier.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Other minors who are soldiers are overseas performing military service, and they have not an opportunity of voting in their own country. The particular case of minor we are dealing with never proceeded overseas. Surely that is a distinction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There is no doubt that, if we could do more for the minor who has gone overseas and is performing a service, than we are doing, we would be glad to do it, and no doubt, if we were to weigh the real merits of each one, this minor is entitled to a great deal more gratitude than the boy who has not been called upon to serve, but we have to consider the case of the boy who volunteered his services and who, so far as depended upon himself, made himself a soldier.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Even in the case in which the parents were obliged to ask for his discharge because he was under eighteen? There are many such cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I do not know to what extent that would occur. It is inevitable that, if we are to make a law of general

application, there will be some instances in which, perhaps, the're may be reasons why it is more difficult to justify the granting of a vote than is the case, speaking generally; but we have to make a rule that is going to be generally applicable, and 1 do not think we can go so far as to discriminate between individual soldiers. The only safe rule is this: A man-was a soldier or he was not a soldier; if he was a soldier, he ought to have the vote, and I do not think, speaking generally, he ought to be deprived of that vote because, although he had been a soldier, at some period before he was enabled to go overseas and become actively engaged, it was ascertained that he was not suitable for a soldier and he was discharged.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Surely the minister would not call a man a soldier who was never accepted as a soldier?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: A man who was not accepted as a soldier never was a soldier and never was a discharged soldier, so that he would not come within the scope of this Bill. We are dealing with soldiers who. actually are soldiers and soldiers who were soldiers and were honourably discharged. A man who was stopped at the outset and was never taken on the strength was not a soldier at all and does not come under this Bill.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Will men of the ages of 20 in classes one and two, who are called out for active service under the Military Service Act, have the right to vote as soon as they are called out? Will a minor who is conscripted have the right to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Perhaps the best answer that I can give is to compare the two measures and see whether the hon. gentleman is right or not. In the drawing up of this Bill we were endeavouring to cover all the methods by which a man might have become a soldier, because we wanted to cover every soldier. We had not presented to our minds in any particular way the provisions of the Military Service Act, and if on comparing them the result would be produced that, by reason of the wording as it stands here, the conclusion would have to be reached that, when a whole class of men from 20 to 34 would be called out for active service, before any individual man came to participate in any way in military operations, this wording would give him a vote, that result was not intended to be produced, and if the combined wording of the two Acts would produce that
result, we should have to find a remedy for that condition of affairs.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Will the minister explain about the motor boat patrol service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I understand that the Motor Boat Patrol Service is an Imperial Service manned by Canadians, their principal work being to patrol the seas that are infested by submarines.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There is no such thing as a Canadian Motor Boat Patrol Service? I understand there are quite a number of men in Halifax at present who belong to this service. They have been there all winter, but as there are no boats for them, they have been doing nothing for some months. Do I understand these men are in the Imperial service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I understand that the Auxiliary Motor Boat Patrol is an Imperial service. If it were a Canadian service we would consider them to be included. I understand that our Canadian service includes the Canadian Expeditionary Force, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Militia on active service, and the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve. The others are all Imperial services.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think that a great number of the men who went across for the Auxiliary Motor Boat Patrol joined the Imperial Navy, and I think they should be given the vote.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am not objecting to their being given the vote.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think we should amend the clause by adding "The Royal Navy."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: With regard to the Imperial service, it is our intention to modify the section by making a provision giving Canadian citizens in the Imperial service, whether naval or military, the right to vote. There may'be difficulty in the way of exercising that right, but they will be given the right.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Clause 3 says:
(1)	Every military elector shall be qualified and entitled to vote at a general election.
(2)	If he can state the electoral district wherein he last continuously resided during at
least	 months of the year immediately
preceding his appointment, enlistment, enrolment or calling out on active service, or so particularly specify a place or places within an electoral district whereat during such period of time he so resided that such electoral

district can therefrom be ascertained, he shall be deemed an elector of the electoral district so stated or to be ascertained.
Suppose that military elector, either in error, or deliberately for political purposes, declares that he had resided during those four months in my constituency, (when really he had resided in the constituency of my hon. friend. Suppose that fifty or a hundred electors make the same mistake, either intentionally or deliberately, could the election be contested on that ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We should have to rely on the strength of their affidavits, for the information on which they are entitled to vote. If I am not mistaken, that is the system in Alberta and Saskatchewan to-day.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Suppose he makes a false affidavit?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The ballot would have to be counted for the time being, just as in Canada, when a man makes a false oath, his ballot is deposited in the box, and not being susceptible of indentification, is no doubt .counted. I presume that upon a contestation of an election, if it could be Shown that a number of votes wrongfully designating an electoral constituency had been polled sufficient to effect the result in a particular constituency, that might be a proper ground for contestation. To-day, of course, a man who has no vote at all, if he commits perjury and swears to his aright to vote, will get a vote, and his ballot Twill be deposited in the box and counted. To find a practical remedy is pretty difficult. Similarly, if under this Act, a man swore that he resided in one place, when he resided in another, I do not think it would be possible to control that at the time of voting. In this election, just as in the elections in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, we shall have to rely for tliis information on the truthfulness of the soldier when put upon his oath.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Is there any provision in the law that would cover such a case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I will look into it.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I was going to move that this clause be amended by striking out the words "whether or not." If this amendment was agreed to the clause would read "military elector" means and includes every person male or female, who, being a British subject, ordinarily resident in Canada." I understand, however, that the minister is not quite sure whether my hon. friend

from St. James is correct in saying that the result of this section would be that the moment the proclamation issued under the Military Service Act every young man in Canada would ipso facto become a military elector, and be entitled to vote. I think a little reflection will convince the minister that my hon. friend is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am inclined to think he is.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Under the Military Service Act the Governor in Council issues a proclamation calling out-that is the word used-all the single men in Canada between certain ages. The effect of this clause would be to make every young man of twenty years of age a military elector, and give him the right to vote. As the minister is inclined to agree with that view, perhaps this clause might stand.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
One branch in which
some Canadians have enlisted is not included in the Bill, and that is the Royal Kite Balloon Branch. If you are going to include all branches of the service, you had better include that branch with the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I should be sorry to omit any.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is a branch of the service which some Canadians joined when they went across the water.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It is included in the Air Service.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: *It has been suggested by some gentlemen during the course of the discussion that the Fisheries Protection Service is connected, departmentally speaking, with the Royal Canadian Navy. A large number of these boats are engaged, in that service, along the coast, quite a number of men being employed. A number of the men so employed are under the age of 21 years. I am not1 objecting to their votes being taken, if it is a proper thing to do. However, I should like to know from the minister if it is fns intention to give votes under this legislation to men who are not engaged actually in the war, but who are employed upon these fisheries protection boats along the coast?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I do not think they
would come under any of these designations. There is the Fisheries Protection Service, and there is the Royal Canadian Navy, which, I understand, is a separate service. I understand, however, from the

Minister of Marine and Fisheries that a large number of boats that would in peace times be engaged in purely fisheries pro-tetction service have been engaged in doing work in the nature of naval service, patrolling the coast and doing trying work under difficult conditions-conditions in which the men in the boats are exposed to serious danger. The crews of such fisheries boats would, I understand, come under the designation herein provided.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Most of the dangerous work performed in connection with patrolling is done by the American boats. Everybody in the Maritime Provinces knows that the boats of the Royal Canadian Navy are doing inshore service. The member for Guysborough is quite right; the men employed in the fisheries boats under the Naval Department are not at all in any position of danger.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I shall get that cleared up. I do not want to cover anybody who is not really doing what may properly be described as naval serviice.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I understand that the minister is to pay some attention to the point raised by the member for St. James f Division (Mr. L. A. Lapointe) in' connection with this proposed legislation. Upon the proclamation in connection with the Conscription Bill being published, every man between the ages of 20 and 35, both inclusive, will become a soldier, and, under the Soldiers' Voting Act, will have the right to vote. But a great many of them could never pass the test which must be passed before they can become soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I shall lay together the texts of the two Bills, and if what the member for St. James Division suggestion may be brought about, I shall take measures so to modify this legislation as to exclude the result that is apprehended.

subsubtopic: SECOND READING OF BILL AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If the proclamation is issued before the election these men become military electors and poll their votes accordingly. But when they come to be examined, many of those who have polled their votes may be pronounced medically unfit, and can never be soldiers. Others may make application, under the law, for exemption. The men exempted have voted, being military voters within the meaning of the law, but they can never be soldiers. Such conditions will arise unless some steps are taken to prevent them. I listened very attentively to everything that was said tonight. As I listened to the various objections and to the answers given, I could not help thinking that the Prime Minister, if he were here, would feel more strongly confirmed than ever in what he said in this House on January 22 last as it appears on page 37 of the revised Hansard. If any hon. gentlemen on this side should say that to take this vote is a practical impossibility, he would find himself backed up by what the Prime Minister said on the occasion referred to. This is what the right hon. gentleman said:
I know something of the conditions at the front, and I venture to put this thought before the House and the country; the men at the front will be not only practically, but actually, disfranchised if an election does take place in this country while they are in the trenches. That is my conviction. I say they would be actually disfranchised because, although I render every tribute to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the committee which had in hand the preparation of the Soldiers' Voting Act of 1915, X am not disposed to think that the arrangements made in that Act or in any other Act that couldl be devised are such as to enable those men to vote, of at least any considerable number of them. You cannot predict what conditions may exist. Suppose an election came on in this country when the fiercest drive of the war was taking place. Do you imagine that the paymasters of those regiments and their commanding officers could busy themselves with handing out ballots to men whose souls were engrossed and whose lives w%re at stake in the enterprise in which they were engaged? There is something more than that. These men at the front have it not in their disposition ; they have it not in their heart or their soul to consider matters of party controversy under the conditions with which they are there confronted. I believe those men would want to put aside any one who came to talk to them about political issues or partisan controversy, under conditions of life or of death, of victory or of defeat such as confront them in the trenches or while making a drive to bring this war to an end. Further than that, there may be perhaps a hundred thousand men not in France. You might be able to have some of those men vote for Government or for Opposition, not for a candidate, as provided in the Act alluded to; but do you imagine that those men who are putting their lives to the supreme test in going overseas to fight for their country, will be greatly interested in political issues, or that they will desire to hear political speeches, or that they will welcome the distribution of partisan literature? I am not saying whether or not these considerations should determine the issue, but I do say that they are considerations that must be taken into account by every member of this Parliament when upon him the responsibility falls as to whether or not there shall be a general election during this war, and I leave it at that.
The Prime Minister argues that it would he impossible with any degree of practicability to take the vote of the soldiers. When the Act of 1915 was before the House

and before the committee I expressed that opinion, and I still hold the view that it would be absolutely impossible with any degree of fairness or justice to take the vote of the soldiers in the manner proposed.
Men have joined regiments and remained with them for a few days or a few months for the purpose of making up the number and starting the battalion. Though not physically fit these men have been allowed to join but they never intended to go overseas. Does the minister think that a man who was not physically fit but who was allowed to join to give the battalion a start should have a vote whereas a man of the same age, 20 years, who is working in a munitions factory, doing excellent work, or who is working in a coal mine, getting out the coal for the manufacture of steel, cannot vote because he is not of age? The man down in the coal mine is more deserving in my judgment than the man who may have been loitering around doing nothing for some weeks in connection with some regiment and who, because he has got the name of being a soldier, is to be entitled to vote. The points taken up by these hon. gentlemen are full of meat and call for the consideration of the minister. I make the broad statement, and I think it will be regarded as, a non-partisan and fair statement, that no man should vote in Canada unless his name is duly on a list somewhere in Canada where he had a right to get his name on the list. If a man who has a right to vote in British Columbia is in Halifax, let his vote be taken there by a proper officer and sent back to British Columbia. I would not take the responsibility of requiring him to go home and vote unless that were considered best although in many cases persons under these circumstances can go home to vote. But I do submit that no man or woman in Canada should be permitted to go to the poll and poll a vote unless the name of that person is properly found on some list. I have always had the notion that the theory of this legislation is that the war should not deprive anybody of a vote who could vote if there were no war. I would not like to see anybody deprived of the right to vote who could have voted if there had been no war, but I am not very much enamoured of the idea that the mere fact that there is a war should qualify people to vote who otherwise are not qualified. Any person who has not yet left Canada has not, in my judgment, qualified himself, to be an elector if he otherwise could not be. It is for that reason 1 say that no man 
should vote in Canada unless his name is properly entered on some list or unless he has a right to vote in some municipal polling division. If the minister will so provide I think he will go a long way toward getting confidence for his Act; that is that no person should vote in Canada unless his name is on some list. Let him make provision that every man who is entitled to vote shall vote and let him make it plain that there shall be no wholesale vote making amongst those who, if there were no war, could not have exercised the franchise. The test should be that no man should be deprived of the franchise who could have voted if there had not been any war. Otherwise, under this Act, you are going to open the door to a class of persons to exercise the franchise because of the war who may never have any interest in this country except that they happen to be in the ranks, many of them because it suits them better than anything else. When the Civil War was on in the United States hundreds of thousands of our young men went to the United States, enlisted and fought because they wanted to get the pa/ and not because we in Canada had any enthusiasm as between the North and South. There are millions of men in this world who are soldiers, that is their business; that is their training. They come to do soldiering for Canada because there is po soldiering going on in any other country that suits them as well, but that dqes not entitle them to claim the right to have a say as to what will happen in this country. The minister was mixing two principles this evening in connection with the franchise. He said that he does not know the difference between a man who is fighting and yet had no residence in Canada and the man who has property in Canada and is a non-resident. The minister knows well that British institutions and law always recognize the right of property, almost as great a right as any which a man can possess. Wherever a man has property he has the right to vote for the purpose of protecting that property. That is why, in the smaller municipal elections, a man owning property in a certain polling district has the right to go and vote and take part in the election of councillor for this district. He has the right to see the man elected who has to deal with his property. That is an underlying principle. The man who has property in the country, if he is a British subject, although residing outside, has the right to come in and vote and to say who shall make the laws govern-

ing that property. But that is entirely different from the man who has no stake in the country, who may come as a professional soldier while the war is on, and who, when the war is over, will leave and will never be seen 'again. I hope the minister will consider some of the points raised by the hon. members to whose remarks I have been addressing myself, and that he will give some attention to the suggestion that people residing in Canada should not be given the right to vote unless they are qualified in some district in which they have a right to be qualified.
